SGA calls on university to publicize its finances, echoing encampment-era demand

The student government adopted its first resolution for DePaul to disclose its finances and passed another to require ID for certain campus buildings after 6 p.m.
Maya Ang, SGA Beat Writer
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:55
Instaread
September 24, 2026
Lily Skinner
SGA president Angelina Squeo speaks during the group’s general body meeting in McGowan South on Wednesday, Sept.16, 2026. SGA passed its first resolution of the year calling on the university to disclose its financial activities.

As promised during their campaigns, the new DePaul Student Government Association cabinet began the school year with a direct challenge to the university administration. 

On Wednesday, Sept. 16, the SGA unanimously adopted its first resolution demanding the university disclose its finances, echoing a demand from student groups during the 2024 encampment. 

The resolution, titled Resolution Calling for Financial Transparency and Accountability in University Investments, calls upon the university’s “moral responsibility” and “Vincentian mission” to publicize its financial activities. 

SGA treasurer Layth Awadallah said this resolution follows over a decade of pro-Palestine student groups asking the university to divest from weapons manufacturers. However, the resolution does not claim that the university is currently invested in such companies. 

In a statement to The DePaulia, university communications said DePaul does not directly invest in stocks or bonds, but DePaul president Robert Manuel “is happy to meet with SGA leadership, along with senior members of the administration” to learn more about the resolution.

It added the university asks its third-party fund managers to adhere to the United Nations’ Principles of Responsible Investing.

The resolution was sponsored by president Angelina Squeo, vice president Muaz Hussaini and Awadallah. The Council on American Islamic Relations helped write the resolution, Awadallah said. 

Last spring, the SGA announced a partnership with the Muslim advocacy organization’s legal representatives as a part of its “community support network.” The organization filed a discrimination complaint with the Illinois Department of Human Rights on behalf of two Palestinian DePaul students in April.

Their proposed “community support network” is still in development. It would “give students a direct line to representation when they’re being discriminated against,” according to Squeo.

Hussaini said he’s noticed discrimination on campus happen “especially with Muslim students, but other students as well.” 

Seniors like Squeo are part of the last current class at DePaul who witnessed the 2024 encampment. The event continues to shape student activism on campus nearly three years later.

The DePaul chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine has led the “DePaul Divest” movement on campus for years. Awadallah said that the group’s two-year suspension in spring spurred the SGA to bring this resolution forward.

Signed by Squeo, the resolution was sent to the Office of the Provost and Office of the President Sept. 18. Squeo said administration would “ideally” allow her to explain the resolution to the Board of Trustees. The SGA has requested a response within 30 days, she said. Members of the SGA and other organizations are currently in talks about possible next steps should the university fail to respond. 

At the university’s annual convocation ceremony on Sept. 2, Manuel said DePaul “cannot stay neutral” on social issues.

Regarding Manuel’s speech, Squeo said, “If we can’t stay neutral, why can’t we disclose our finances and see what we’re investing in? That’s why we’re pushing this resolution.”

Since its new cabinet was elected in the spring, the SGA has had very limited interaction with university administration, Squeo said.

Squeo and Hussaini ran as write-ins in the spring, winning 56% of the vote. Voter turnout mounted to about 6% of the student population, a significant increase compared to recent years.

Squeo, in part, attributes the results to their endorsement by DePaul’s Young Democratic Socialists of America Chapter. The Squeo-Hussaini campaign really aligned with YDSA values, according to Hussaini.

The SGA still intends to work alongside YDSA in its campaigns and initiatives, according to Squeo. 

Awadallah said the SGA is working to “build up” student activist group campaigns, including the Young Democratic Socialists of America, Students Against Incarceration, Native American & Indigenous Student Association, Palestinian Cultural Association and Southwest Asian North African Club, among others. 

“SGA stands as a body that should be in support of anything any student organization does,” Squeo said. “Whether it be our stance or not, we’re students at the end of the day. So we’re here for each other.”

When asked about the new cabinet’s policy stance, Squeo noted that SGA isn’t directly standing against the university administration.

“It’s us standing for the students, and sometimes that means we’re not going to be in direct alignment.”

Proposed evening ID access for certain campus buildings closer to full approval 

On Wednesday, Sept. 23, SGA adopted its second resolution of the year, proposing  a pilot program that would require a valid DePaul ID to enter certain campus buildings after 6 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends.

The pilot program is intended to reduce unauthorized access by people who are not affiliated with or enrolled at DePaul and to enhance campus safety, according to the resolution.

Lincoln Park buildings in the proposal include: McGowan North, McGowan South, Arts & Letters, the Schmidt Academic Center, the Levan Center, O’Connell Hall and Byrne Hall. 

Loop campus buildings in the proposal include: the Lewis Center, CDM Center and the Richard M. and Maggie C. Daley Building.
